title: Trump Backs Proposed $103,000 H-1B Fee in Labor Day Proclamation
excerpt: The Department of Homeland Security's proposed $103,265 fee on cap-subject H-1B petitions, promoted by Trump in his Labor Day message, could combine with an earlier blocked fee to push total visa costs past $200,000.
body:
• President Trump used his 2026 Labor Day proclamation to promote a proposed $103,265 fee on cap-subject H-1B visa petitions, framing it as a measure to protect American workers.
  • The Department of Homeland Security published the proposed rule in August, with public comments due September 24. The fee would be added on top of existing application costs.
  • A separate $100,000 H-1B fee imposed by Trump in September 2025 was struck down by a federal judge in June as unlawful. If both fees are eventually upheld, total costs could exceed $200,000 per petition.
  • Indian nationals, the largest group of H-1B beneficiaries, would be disproportionately affected by the proposed fee increase.

H-1B Fees Take Center Stage in Labor Day Message

President Donald Trump used his 2026 Labor Day proclamation to explicitly promote a proposed new fee on H-1B visa petitions, directly linking immigration policy to his broader agenda of protecting American workers and boosting domestic manufacturing.

https://x.com/yespunjab/status/2097189621159637428

“To ensure we are hiring and training American workers, we are proposing a new fee on H-1B visa petitions that will encourage companies to invest in qualified Americans before looking overseas for labor,” Trump said in the proclamation, signed September 4 and designating September 7 as Labor Day.

The presidential endorsement places the politically sensitive H-1B visa program squarely into what is traditionally a celebration of American labor, signaling the administration’s intent to keep immigration restrictions at the center of its economic agenda.

The $103,265 Proposed Fee

The fee Trump referenced is a $103,265 charge proposed by the Department of Homeland Security in August for all H-1B petitions subject to the annual numerical cap, including petitions eligible for the advanced-degree exemption. Under the proposed rule, the fee would be paid when the petition is filed and would come on top of existing application fees that typically range from $2,000 to $5,000.

DHS says the revenue would help cover federal costs associated with administering the immigration system. The proposal is projected to generate $8.8 billion over a decade, with funding distributed across USCIS, ICE, CBP, the immigration court system, the Labor Department, and the State Department, according to USA Today.

Public comments on the proposed rule are due by September 24, 2026. The proposal drew more than 5,000 comments in its first week alone, reflecting the program’s political sensitivity.

Legal Battle Over Prior $100,000 Fee

The proposed $103,265 fee is separate from a $100,000 H-1B fee Trump imposed through executive proclamation in September 2025. That earlier fee targeted new H-1B visas for workers entering the United States from abroad.

U.S. District Judge Leo Sorokin in Massachusetts struck down the $100,000 fee in June, ruling it was “arbitrary and capricious” and that the proclamation “does not provide any explanation for imposing a tax on employers.” The First Circuit Court of Appeals refused to block Sorokin’s ruling in July while the government appeals.

“This is just a way to kill the H-1B program. This is just one of the many nails in the coffin of legal immigration in this country.”

— Shev Dalal-Dheini, Senior Director of Government Relations, American Immigration Lawyers Association

If both fees are eventually upheld, employers could face a combined cost exceeding $200,000 per H-1B petition, according to USA Today. During the five months the $100,000 fee was in effect before being blocked, only 85 new applications were filed from abroad — an 87% drop — and the government collected $28 million less than it would have under the previous fee structure.

Impact on Indian Professionals and Tech Companies

Indian nationals have historically constituted the largest group of H-1B beneficiaries, making any changes to the program closely watched in India and among the Indian professional community in the United States. Amazon, Apple, Google, and Meta collectively employed nearly 19,000 H-1B workers through June 30, according to USCIS data.

The H-1B program distributes 85,000 new visas per year under a congressional cap. Universities and nonprofit research centers are excluded from the cap and hire tens of thousands more foreign workers. Immigration advocacy group FWD.us estimates there are 730,000 H-1B holders currently in the country, along with 550,000 dependents.

Supporters of the higher fees argue they level the playing field for American workers. “The lower effective cost of sponsoring foreign labor has repeatedly put American candidates at a disadvantage,” wrote Benjamin Wolf, a technology professional in Reston, Virginia, in a public comment supporting the proposal.

What Comes Next

The $103,265 fee remains a proposed rule, not an immediately applicable charge. After the September 24 comment deadline, the administration would need to decide whether and how to finalize the rule. Unlike Trump’s earlier executive proclamation, this proposal is being pursued through the formal federal rulemaking process, which could provide stronger legal footing but also takes longer to implement.

Meanwhile, the legal battle over the original $100,000 fee continues at the First Circuit. The Justice Department argues the fee was designed to “regulate immigration, not to raise revenue,” and that the president has “inherent authority to exclude aliens from entering the nation.”

For Indian professionals and their employers, the combined effect of proposed and pending fees, alongside tighter wage requirements and increased USCIS scrutiny, represents a fundamental restructuring of the cost of doing business through the H-1B program.
